$comment: The FINISHED config for the DbScrubTest fixture — what dbscrubtest.masking.json becomes after you run `report`, paste its UNCLASSIFIED block back, and pick a real strategy for each column. Every live column resolves to a verdict, so a clean run passes verify and earns the stamp. Keep the incomplete one too: the pair is the whole workflow, and the difference between them is exactly what the verify gate catches.

tables.$comment: The kitchen-sink table. FullName is computed and ValidFrom/ValidTo are GENERATED ALWAYS, so all three are exempt — SQL Server maintains them and would reject the UPDATE anyway.
tables.name: dbo.Person

columns.$comment: Free text, and the reason the gate exists. The seed data hides a phone number and a second email inside prose, where no shape-preserving strategy would help — scrambling it would keep both shapes intact. Replace the lot.
columns.name: Notes

columns.$comment: A computed column: FirstName + ' ' + LastName. It cannot be written, and it holds whatever those two hold — so masking them masks this automatically. Listed only because dbscrub still asks for a verdict on computed columns.
columns.name: FullName
columns.reason: computed from FirstName and LastName, both masked

tables.$comment: CDC-tracked, in a non-dbo schema. Its Notes column interpolates a person's email address, which is the classic way PII escapes into a table nobody thinks of as holding any.
tables.name: app.Enrollment

tables.$comment: Audit table: truncated, never masked (DECISIONS.md D5). Its Payload column holds JSON with an email and an SSN inside it, and no column-level rule can reach in there.
tables.name: dbo.LoginAudit

tables.$comment: A HEAP — no primary key. Every strategy here is the same for every row, which is what makes a keyless table maskable at all: one set-based UPDATE, one transaction. "scramble" would be refused here (DECISIONS.md D19).
tables.name: dbo.ContactImport
